CAIRO, Egypt (CNN)  -- Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak met Thursday in Cairo amid escalating cross-border violence between Israel and Hamas. Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni meets Thursday with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in Cairo. The session follows the end of a tenuous 6-month-long cease-fire between the Israeli military and Hamas militants in Gaza. Egypt mediated the first truce and is trying to negotiate an extension despite what Israel says are dozens of rockets fired by Hamas into the Jewish state this week. Livni criticized Hamas after her meeting with Mubarak. "Hamas needs to understand that Israel's basic desire to live in a tranquil region doesn't mean that Israel is willing to accept ongoing shooting at its population," she said, according to the Israeli Foreign Ministry. "Enough is enough. We cannot accept this situation, and the situation will change." Egypt expressed concern about a deteriorating humanitarian situation in Gaza, an Israeli Foreign Ministry statement said. The Egyptian Foreign Ministry said this week that it would help countries and organizations deliver aid through Egyptian territory to Palestinians in Gaza. Livni also met with the head of Egyptian intelligence Thursday and is scheduled to talk with the Egyptian foreign minister. Israeli military officials said Hamas militants fired more than 65 rockets into southern Israel on Wednesday. Meanwhile, the Israeli air force said it killed a Hamas militant who was part of a group launching the rockets into Israel. An Israeli police spokesman said no one had been injured in the latest barrage of rocket attacks. But emergency workers with Magen David Adom, Israel's Red Cross agency, treated 57 people suffering from shock, half of them children, an agency official said, adding that 200 ambulances were standing by in the area. "I think the circumstances are extremely tragic, that Muslim zealots of Hamas have decided to shatter and ruin the Christmas celebrations of the Christian brothers in the Holy Land, both in the West Bank and of course in Gaza itself," Israeli Welfare Minister Isaac Herzog said. "If things deteriorate further, then of course we'll have to take necessary action, which will be very painful," Herzog said, adding that civilians had gathered in shelters in southern Israel to try to stay safe amid the rocket attacks. Asked about the possibility of Israel coming up with a new strategy, Herzog responded, "The new strategy could be, of course, an all-out conflict against Hamas, which is a possibility that voices in Israel are calling for. We are trying to show restraint." Hamas is a Palestinian Islamic fundamentalist organization whose military wing, Izzedine al Qassam, has admitted responsibility for terrorist attacks against Israeli civilians as well as attacks against the Israeli military. Israel and the U.S. State Department consider Hamas a terrorist organization, though it also operates an extensive social services network in the territories. Mark Regev, spokesman for Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert, said, "Our position is clear: We will answer quiet with quiet, and we will answer attacks with measures designed to protect our people." Olmert has threatened to respond to the ongoing attacks. The truce between the Hamas government in Gaza and Israel expired Friday. Under the Egyptian-brokered deal, Hamas agreed to end militant attacks on Israel from Gaza, and Israel agreed to halt raids inside the territory and ease its blockade on humanitarian goods. In reality, the truce had started breaking down two months ago. Rocket attacks by militants became more frequent, and Israel resumed airstrikes inside Gaza. "We really appreciate the Egyptian efforts. ...," Herzog said. "The Egyptians have tried endlessly and tirelessly in the past few weeks to bring Hamas back to cease-fire mode." Olmert said Sunday that Israel will "take the necessary measures" to respond to the rocket attacks and "will know when to respond correctly and with the necessary responsibility." "A responsible government is neither eager for battle, nor does it shy away from it," he said.

**CAIRO, Egypt (CNN) —** Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni met with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in Cairo on Thursday amid escalating cross-border violence between Israel and Hamas.

The meeting followed the expiration of a tenuous six-month cease-fire between the Israeli military and Hamas militants in Gaza. Egypt brokered the original truce and is seeking to negotiate an extension, despite what Israel says were dozens of rockets fired by Hamas into the Jewish state this week.

Following her meeting with Mubarak, Livni criticized Hamas.

“Hamas needs to understand that Israel's basic desire to live in a tranquil region doesn't mean that Israel is willing to accept ongoing shooting at its population,” she said, according to the Israeli Foreign Ministry. “Enough is enough. We cannot accept this situation, and the situation will change.”

Egypt expressed concern about the deteriorating humanitarian situation in Gaza, according to a statement from the Israeli Foreign Ministry. The Egyptian Foreign Ministry said this week that it would help countries and organizations deliver aid through Egyptian territory to Palestinians in Gaza.

Livni also met Thursday with the head of Egyptian intelligence and was scheduled to hold talks with the Egyptian foreign minister.

Israeli military officials said Hamas militants fired more than 65 rockets into southern Israel on Wednesday. Meanwhile, the Israeli air force said it killed a Hamas militant who was part of a group launching rockets into Israel.

An Israeli police spokesman said no one had been injured in the latest barrage. However, emergency workers with Magen David Adom, Israel's Red Cross agency, treated 57 people suffering from shock, half of them children, an agency official said. The official added that 200 ambulances were standing by in the area.

“I think the circumstances are extremely tragic, that Muslim zealots of Hamas have decided to shatter and ruin the Christmas celebrations of the Christian brothers in the Holy Land, both in the West Bank and of course in Gaza itself,” Israeli Welfare Minister Isaac Herzog said.

“If things deteriorate further, then of course we'll have to take necessary action, which will be very painful,” Herzog said, adding that civilians had gathered in shelters in southern Israel to protect themselves from the rocket attacks.

Asked whether Israel might adopt a new strategy, Herzog responded, “The new strategy could be, of course, an all-out conflict against Hamas, which is a possibility that voices in Israel are calling for. We are trying to show restraint.”

Hamas is a Palestinian Islamic fundamentalist organization whose military wing, Izzedine al Qassam, has claimed responsibility for terrorist attacks against Israeli civilians, as well as attacks against the Israeli military. Israel and the U.S. State Department consider Hamas a terrorist organization, although it also operates an extensive social-services network in the territories.

Mark Regev, spokesman for Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert, said, “Our position is clear: We will answer quiet with quiet, and we will answer attacks with measures designed to protect our people.”

Olmert has threatened to respond to the continuing attacks.

The truce between the Hamas government in Gaza and Israel expired Friday. Under the Egyptian-brokered agreement, Hamas pledged to end militant attacks on Israel from Gaza, while Israel agreed to halt raids inside the territory and ease its blockade on humanitarian goods.

In practice, however, the truce had begun to unravel two months earlier. Rocket attacks by militants became more frequent, and Israel resumed airstrikes inside Gaza.

“We really appreciate the Egyptian efforts. ...,” Herzog said. “The Egyptians have tried endlessly and tirelessly in the past few weeks to bring Hamas back to cease-fire mode.”

Olmert said Sunday that Israel would “take the necessary measures” in response to the rocket attacks and “will know when to respond correctly and with the necessary responsibility.”

“A responsible government is neither eager for battle, nor does it shy away from it,” he said.

CAIRO, Egypt (CNN) — Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni held talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in Cairo on Thursday as violence between Israel and Hamas intensified across the border.

Their meeting came after a fragile six-month ceasefire between Israeli forces and Hamas fighters in Gaza expired. Egypt, which brokered the original agreement, is seeking to extend it, even as Israel reports that Hamas launched dozens of rockets into Israeli territory this week.

After speaking with Mubarak, Livni condemned Hamas. In remarks reported by Israel’s Foreign Ministry, she said Hamas should not mistake Israel’s wish for regional calm as a willingness to tolerate continued attacks on its citizens. She added that Israel had reached its limit, could no longer accept the circumstances, and intended to change them.

According to an Israeli Foreign Ministry statement, Egypt raised concerns about the worsening humanitarian conditions in Gaza. Egypt’s Foreign Ministry said this week that it would assist governments and organizations in transporting aid through Egyptian territory to Palestinians in Gaza.

Livni also met Thursday with Egypt’s intelligence chief and was due to hold discussions with the Egyptian foreign minister.

Israeli military authorities said Hamas fighters launched more than 65 rockets toward southern Israel on Wednesday. At the same time, the Israeli air force reported killing a Hamas member who belonged to a group firing rockets into Israel.

An Israeli police representative said the latest rocket assault caused no injuries. However, Magen David Adom, Israel’s Red Cross organization, provided treatment to 57 people for shock, about half of whom were children. An agency official also said 200 ambulances had been placed on standby in the region.

Israeli Welfare Minister Isaac Herzog described the situation as deeply tragic, accusing Hamas’s Muslim extremists of destroying Christmas celebrations for Christians in the Holy Land, including those in the West Bank and Gaza.

Herzog warned that Israel would have to take necessary and highly painful steps if conditions worsened further. He also said civilians in southern Israel had taken refuge in shelters to protect themselves from the rockets.

When asked whether Israel might adopt a different approach, Herzog said one possibility was a full-scale confrontation with Hamas, an option being advocated by some people in Israel. He emphasized, however, that Israel was attempting to exercise restraint.

Hamas is a Palestinian fundamentalist Islamic group. Its armed branch, Izzedine al Qassam, has claimed responsibility for terrorist attacks targeting Israeli civilians and for assaults on Israel’s military. Both Israel and the U.S. State Department classify Hamas as a terrorist organization, although the group also runs a broad social-welfare system in the Palestinian territories.

Mark Regev, spokesman for Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert, said Israel’s policy was straightforward: calm would be met with calm, while attacks would prompt actions intended to defend the Israeli population.

Olmert has also warned that Israel will respond to the continuing rocket fire.

The Egyptian-mediated ceasefire between Israel and the Hamas administration in Gaza officially ended on Friday. Under its terms, Hamas pledged to stop attacks launched from Gaza against Israel. In return, Israel agreed to end military incursions into Gaza and relax restrictions on humanitarian supplies entering the territory.

In practice, however, the agreement had begun unraveling two months earlier. Militants increased the frequency of rocket launches, while Israel restarted airstrikes in Gaza.

Herzog said Israel greatly valued Egypt’s work, noting that Egyptian officials had made persistent efforts during the preceding weeks to persuade Hamas to return to a ceasefire.

On Sunday, Olmert said Israel would take whatever action was required in response to the rocket attacks and would choose the appropriate time to act responsibly. He added that a responsible government neither seeks war nor avoids it when necessary.

Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni traveled to Cairo for talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak as violence between Israel and Hamas intensified along the Gaza border. Their discussions focused on Egypt’s attempts to restore the six-month cease-fire between the two sides, curb rocket attacks on southern Israel and ensure that humanitarian supplies could reach Gaza’s increasingly vulnerable population.

The Egyptian-brokered truce had reduced hostilities for several months, but it came under growing strain and eventually expired without being renewed. Hamas accused Israel of failing to ease its restrictions on Gaza, while Israel said Palestinian militants had continued to smuggle weapons and launch rockets. Egypt, which shares a border with Gaza and has long served as a mediator, sought to prevent the confrontation from developing into a broader military conflict.

Tensions rose sharply after Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups fired more than 65 rockets and mortar shells into southern Israel. The attacks disrupted daily life in Israeli communities near Gaza and increased pressure on the Israeli government to respond. Israel subsequently carried out a strike that killed a Hamas militant, further fueling fears of retaliation and escalation.

Speaking after her meeting with Mubarak, Livni said Israel could no longer accept continued attacks on its citizens. She warned that the situation had become intolerable and indicated that Israel was prepared to take stronger action if the rocket fire did not stop. Her remarks reflected the Israeli government’s increasingly forceful position as residents of southern towns sought greater protection.

At the same time, Egypt continued efforts to revive the cease-fire and facilitate the delivery of food, medicine, fuel and other essential goods into Gaza. Border closures and restrictions had worsened shortages in the territory, where civilians were already facing deteriorating living conditions. Humanitarian organizations warned that renewed fighting and reduced access through border crossings would deepen the crisis.

The Cairo meeting underscored the urgency of Egypt’s diplomatic role. With both Israel and Hamas blaming each other for the collapse of the truce, prospects for a quick agreement remained uncertain. Continued rocket fire and Israeli military responses threatened not only to trigger a wider confrontation but also to impose further hardship on civilians on both sides of the border.

## Livni meets Mubarak as Israel-Hamas tensions escalate

**CAIRO, Egypt —** Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni met Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in Cairo amid mounting fears of a broader conflict between Israel and Hamas following the expiration of a six-month cease-fire.

The Egyptian-brokered truce ended December 19, and violence has intensified since then. Palestinian militants have fired rockets and mortars from Gaza into southern Israel, while Israeli forces have carried out strikes and maintained tight restrictions on the territory’s border crossings.

Speaking after the meeting, Livni warned that Israel would not tolerate continued attacks on its citizens.

“Enough is enough,” she said, accusing Hamas of undermining regional stability and holding Gaza’s residents hostage to its militant agenda. Livni said Israel wanted peace but would act to defend communities within range of Palestinian rockets.

Mubarak called for restraint and urged both sides to avoid steps that could lead to a major military confrontation. Egypt, which borders Gaza and has served as a key intermediary between Israel and Hamas, has been pressing for renewed calm.

Hamas officials blamed Israel for the collapse of the cease-fire, citing military operations in Gaza and the continued blockade of the territory. Israel says the restrictions are intended to prevent weapons and materials that could be used in attacks from reaching Hamas.

The surge in rocket fire has disrupted daily life in southern Israeli towns, where residents have repeatedly sought shelter. In Gaza, residents are preparing for the possibility of a large-scale Israeli response as humanitarian conditions continue to deteriorate.

Diplomatic efforts remain complicated by the fact that Israel and several Western governments consider Hamas a terrorist organization and refuse to deal with it directly. Egypt has continued indirect contacts with the group in an effort to restore the truce.

The Cairo meeting came as Israeli leaders weighed their options, warning that continued attacks could trigger significant military action in the densely populated Gaza Strip.

counterfactuals.output:
**Egypt Pushes to Revive Gaza Truce After Renewed Fighting**

*Historical breaking-news style report based on the 2014 Gaza conflict; statements are paraphrased where exact wording cannot be independently verified.*

**CAIRO/JERUSALEM —** Egypt intensified diplomatic efforts to restore a ceasefire between Israel and Palestinian factions in Gaza after renewed rocket fire and Israeli airstrikes brought an abrupt end to a temporary truce and disrupted negotiations in Cairo.

Egyptian mediators urged both sides to halt hostilities and return to indirect talks, portraying the Cairo process as the most practical route toward ending the fighting. Palestinian and Israeli delegations had been discussing a longer-term arrangement that could address Israel’s security concerns while easing restrictions on Gaza, but the talks stalled amid disagreements over border crossings, reconstruction, disarmament and guarantees against renewed attacks.

The renewed violence underscored the fragility of Egypt’s mediation. Israel said it responded after rockets were launched from Gaza, while Hamas accused Israel of refusing to meet Palestinian demands, including an end to the blockade. Each side blamed the other for the collapse of the ceasefire.

### Livni backs diplomacy but demands pressure on Hamas

Tzipi Livni, then Israel’s justice minister and a member of the security cabinet, argued that Israel should continue to pursue a diplomatic solution while making clear that Hamas could not obtain political gains through violence.

Livni maintained that any durable arrangement had to weaken Hamas and strengthen more moderate Palestinian institutions, particularly the Palestinian Authority under President Mahmoud Abbas. She also supported international and regional involvement in Gaza’s reconstruction, provided that aid and building materials were monitored and prevented from being diverted to tunnels or weapons production.

Her position reflected divisions within Israel’s governing coalition. Some ministers favored a broader military campaign to remove Hamas from power, while others warned that reoccupying Gaza would impose heavy military, economic and diplomatic costs without guaranteeing a lasting solution.

### Herzog criticizes Netanyahu’s handling of the war

Opposition leader Isaac Herzog criticized Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s management of the crisis, saying the government had failed to translate Israel’s military operations into a clear diplomatic strategy.

Herzog called for closer cooperation with Egypt, the Palestinian Authority and moderate Arab governments. He argued that Abbas should be given a central role in administering Gaza’s border crossings and reconstruction, which could reduce Hamas’s control while offering Gaza’s residents a political and economic alternative.

Although Herzog supported military action to stop rocket attacks, he said force alone could not create long-term security for communities in southern Israel. A sustained ceasefire, he argued, would require regional diplomacy and a broader effort to resolve the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

### Regev: Cairo remains the viable negotiating channel

Israeli government spokesman Mark Regev emphasized that Israel remained open to a ceasefire based on Egyptian mediation. He described the Cairo framework as the principal viable diplomatic channel and said Israel wanted a durable end to rocket fire rather than another short pause that allowed Hamas to regroup.

Regev said Israel had accepted previous Egyptian ceasefire proposals and accused Hamas of repeatedly violating them. He also insisted that any agreement must address the organization’s military capabilities, including rockets and cross-border tunnels.

Israel’s position was that restrictions on Gaza could be eased only alongside credible security measures. Palestinian negotiators, however, sought the reopening of crossings, expanded fishing rights, reconstruction guarantees and relief from the blockade that had constrained Gaza’s economy.

### Olmert attacks government strategy

Former Israeli prime minister Ehud Olmert also criticized Netanyahu’s conduct, contending that the government lacked a coherent political objective and had not made sufficient use of international and regional partnerships.

Olmert argued that Israel should work with Egypt and Abbas rather than allow Hamas to emerge as the primary representative of Palestinian interests in Gaza. His intervention added to mounting domestic debate over whether the military campaign had achieved enough to justify its human and economic costs.

The former premier’s criticism was especially significant because he had led Israel during the 2008–09 Gaza war. He suggested that military pressure had to be linked to a defined diplomatic outcome, warning that otherwise Israel risked returning to the same cycle of rocket fire, airstrikes and temporary truces.

### Egypt seeks to keep negotiations alive

Egypt’s government faced the difficult task of mediating between parties that did not negotiate directly and deeply distrusted one another. Cairo maintained close security ties with Israel but also sought to demonstrate that it could secure meaningful relief for Gaza’s population.

Relations between Egypt and Hamas were particularly strained because Cairo viewed the group as closely connected to the Muslim Brotherhood, which Egyptian authorities had outlawed. Even so, Egypt’s control of the Rafah crossing and its contacts with Israel and Palestinian representatives made it indispensable to any ceasefire effort.

Diplomats said a renewed truce would probably need to proceed in stages: an immediate halt to rocket launches and Israeli strikes, followed by negotiations over crossings, humanitarian access, reconstruction and longer-term security arrangements.

The urgency was heightened by Gaza’s worsening humanitarian conditions. Weeks of conflict had killed civilians, displaced families and damaged homes, hospitals, power facilities and water infrastructure. Israeli communities near Gaza also faced continuing rocket and mortar attacks, forcing residents to remain near shelters and disrupting daily life.

Despite the collapse of the latest pause, Egyptian officials continued pressing both delegations to return to Cairo. Whether those efforts could produce more than another temporary cessation of hostilities depended on the parties’ willingness to accept an incremental agreement—and on Egypt’s ability to bridge demands that remained far apart.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the December 2008 escalation between Israel and Hamas, focusing on Livni’s Cairo talks, the humanitarian situation in Gaza, Hamas rocket attacks, and Israel’s possible military response.
counterfactuals.output:
In late December 2008, the six-month Egyptian-brokered truce between Israel and Hamas expired, triggering a rapid escalation:

- **Livni’s Cairo talks:** Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni met Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in Cairo on December 25. She warned that Israel would no longer tolerate continued rocket fire from Hamas-controlled Gaza. Egypt urged restraint and sought to revive mediation, but Livni indicated that Israel was considering stronger action.
- **Humanitarian conditions in Gaza:** Israel had tightened its blockade and frequently closed Gaza’s crossings in response to rocket attacks. Fuel, food, medicine, electricity, and other basic supplies were increasingly scarce. Aid organizations warned that Gaza’s roughly 1.5 million residents faced a worsening humanitarian crisis. Israel briefly allowed some humanitarian deliveries through while maintaining security restrictions.
- **Hamas rocket attacks:** Palestinian militants, including Hamas, fired dozens of rockets and mortars into southern Israel after the truce ended, reaching communities such as Sderot and Ashkelon. Hamas described the attacks as retaliation for Israeli raids, killings, and the blockade; Israel said the launches made normal civilian life near Gaza impossible.
- **Possible Israeli response:** Israeli leaders said restraint was running out and discussed a major military operation, while also weighing targeted strikes and continued economic pressure. Troops and armor were prepared around Gaza, and the cabinet authorized broader action. Two days after Livni’s Cairo visit, Israel launched **Operation Cast Lead** with extensive airstrikes on Hamas security and government facilities, beginning a three-week war.

CAIRO, Egypt (CNN) — Egyptian officials intensified diplomatic efforts to extend a cease-fire between Israel and Hamas as renewed cross-border violence threatened to derail negotiations and deepen the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.

Egypt, which has served as a key intermediary alongside Qatar, has been pressing both sides to prolong the pause in fighting and agree to further exchanges of hostages held by Hamas for Palestinian prisoners detained by Israel. Negotiators were also seeking guarantees for continued deliveries of food, fuel and medical supplies into Gaza through the Rafah crossing.

The talks came amid reports of rocket fire from Gaza and Israeli military strikes near the border. Israel said it would respond to attacks on its territory, while Hamas accused Israel of violating the terms of the cease-fire. The competing claims could not immediately be independently verified.

Egyptian authorities urged both parties to exercise restraint, warning that a collapse of the truce could trigger a broader escalation and further displacement of Palestinian civilians. Cairo has also reiterated its opposition to any forced movement of Gaza’s population into Egypt’s Sinai Peninsula.

The cease-fire has provided a brief respite after weeks of intense Israeli bombardment and ground operations launched in response to Hamas’ October 7 attack on Israel. Hamas killed civilians and soldiers and took hostages during the assault, according to Israeli authorities. Israel’s subsequent campaign has caused widespread destruction and a mounting Palestinian death toll, according to health officials in Gaza.

International pressure has grown for a longer halt to the fighting. The United Nations and aid organizations say humanitarian needs remain immense despite increased deliveries during the pause.

Negotiations were continuing, but officials cautioned that any extension would depend on agreement over the release of additional hostages and prisoners, as well as adherence to the cease-fire’s security provisions.
